Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection: A Technical Case Study

How an unfamiliar computer-vision problem was investigated: a prototype fitted on defect-free circuit-board images only, which flags new images for a human reviewer. Each controlled change was pre-registered, frozen and tested once on a board type not used in its development; deviations are disclosed. The work is kept reproducible, reviewable and testable for whoever maintains it next.

RecommendationNot ready for production-affecting deployment. Proposed next step: bounded, non-disruptive shadow-mode validation on real line images, subject to site requirements, authorization and appropriate entry checks. Factory access has not been obtained.

Additional finding · separate board type (PCB3)The v2 baseline achieved 90% recall on a separately evaluated PCB category, but remained sensitive to brighter images (false alarms +15.2 pts). A lighting correction tested there is not adopted: it introduced a blur sensitivity. PCB3 experiment →

1Problem and assumptions

Inspection problem
On a production line, defects are rare and varied, so labelled defect examples are usually scarce. For the normal-only pipeline, VisA defect labels and masks are reserved for evaluation and illustration. The separate PCB4 supervised study uses defect annotations for YOLO training. Question: can a model that has only seen good boards send the right images to a reviewer, without burying the reviewer in false alarms?
Working assumptions
  • Review support, not disposition: the tool recommends a human review and never rejects a board, so a false alarm costs reviewer time, not product.
  • One fixed overhead camera, one board type per model; each new board type gets its own fit, board region and threshold.
  • Acceptance targets (recall ≥ 90%, false alarms ≤ 10%, AUROC ≥ 0.90, latency ≤ 1 s) are the developer's proposal, written before any test and never edited after a result.
  • Public benchmark images and synthetic perturbations stand in for a line; they cannot show real lighting drift or a real defect mix.
What is not established
No manufacturing user was involved, no factory image was used, no pilot was run, and no labour saving or financial return was measured. Reported metrics were cross-checked against the recorded per-image scores using a separate verification implementation. AI-assisted technical review was performed; final project-owner review remains pending.

2Dataset and observations

VisA (Amazon Science, CC BY 4.0) provides, per circuit-board type, about a thousand normal images and a hundred defective ones with pixel masks. PCB1 was the development board; PCB2 and PCB3 were each opened only after their protocol was committed.

How every board type is split

  • Fit — normal images the model learns from (600).
  • Calibration — separate normal images that set the threshold, frozen before testing (150).
  • Holdout — extra normal images never used for any choice; a second false-alarm estimate.
  • Official test — the dataset's own test normals and all defects, scored once.

The split is written by a seeded script, audited with file hashes for overlap and duplicates, and committed before modelling. Counts shown are PCB3's.

What inspecting the training images showed

  1. PCB1 Demonstrated

    Boards arrive in different orientations

    116 of 600 training images (19%) were turned half a round; placement and tilt also varied.

    So: Registration (centroid, tilt, and a template check for the half-turn) runs before any modelling.

  2. PCB1 Post hoc

    False alarms came from the background

    All 13/13 false alarms of v1 on PCB1 normals peaked on the cloth (dust, lint), not on the board.

    So: v2 takes the score over the board region only. PCB1 could not confirm this, so it was tested on PCB2.

  3. PCB1 Demonstrated

    A benchmark confound

    Most PCB1 test defects are photographed turned half a round, while most normal boards are not.

    So: A model without registration could score well by detecting orientation instead of defects; registration removes that shortcut.

3Candidate approaches and selection rationale

The need at this stage was a normal-only baseline that can be fitted from defect-free images in minutes, explained to an engineer, and frozen. The table is the selection rationale; the frozen evaluations used only the chosen approach.

ApproachLabels neededOutputFits whenMain risk
Frozen CNN features + per-position Gaussian (chosen)Defect-free images onlyAnomaly score and heat mapDefects are rare and not known in advance; a reviewer stays in the loopMisses subtle defects whose features look normal; sensitive to pose and lighting
Object detector (YOLOv8, YOLO11)Representative box-labelled defect examples; coverage of expected defect variation must be evaluatedGeneric defect bounding boxes and confidence scores; no defect-subtype classification in this experimentRepresentative defect labels are available and defect locations are neededUnseen defect variation can reduce recall (see the experiment below); label availability, labelling cost and upkeep
Fine-tuned classifier or backboneLabelled good and bad imagesImage-level class or scoreEnough labelled defects exist and the process is stableOverfits small defect sets; needs a training, validation and retraining process
Golden-image or rule-based comparisonNone, but tuning per productDifferences from a referenceFixture, lighting and product are tightly controlledBreaks under pose, lighting and normal part-to-part variation

Choosing the normal-only model is a statement about this stage — no defect labels, a reviewer in the loop — not a claim that it beats supervised models. The exploratory detector uses one class, defect: ground-truth segmentation components become bounding boxes; defect subtypes are used for study partitions, not predicted classes.

Testing the alternative: YOLOv8 and YOLO11 on an unused board type Exploratory

Exploratory study — separate from the frozen PCB1–PCB3 evaluations, with its own protocol, data and code. It changes no earlier result or decision.

Instead of relying on descriptions, the main alternative was trained and measured. The protocol was committed before the fourth VisA board type (PCB4) was opened: off-the-shelf YOLOv8s and YOLO11s, fixed default settings, five-fold cross-validation over the 100 defects (80 box-labelled defects per training fold: 64 trained on, 16 for checkpoint selection), and the same task and threshold rule as the project — flag an image for review at a threshold set on 150 separate normal images.

How to read it

  • With labels for the same defect types, both detectors flagged almost every defect: YOLOv8s 98%, YOLO11s 95%, against 60% for the normal-only pipeline, at similar overall false-alarm rates on the test normals (but see the next point). Paired difference YOLO11s − normal-only: +35 pts recall (CI +24 to +45), −1 pts false alarms (CI −4 to +1). The smallest third of defects: 91% versus 47%. The two detectors cannot be ranked on this sample: they disagreed on only a handful of defects (4 caught only by YOLOv8s, 1 only by YOLO11s).
  • Post-hoc checks: image-level flagging and correct localization are separate; an acquisition cue exists. For 89/95 flagged defect images, the box that set YOLO11s's score touched the ground-truth defect grown by 16 px (YOLOv8s 92/98). That definition needs a touching box, not a matching one; at IoU ≥ 0.5 with a ground-truth box the counts are 74/95 and 79/98. An audit found that PCB4 defect images are darker on average than the normal images (brightness alone ranks them with AUROC 0.79), and that YOLO scores on defect-free images rise as images get darker. In a post-hoc exploratory analysis, test normals were reweighted to an artificial distribution matching the defect images' brightness. At the original frozen thresholds, the conditional FPR estimates were 9.0% (YOLOv8s) and 6.9% (YOLO11s), against 2.1% for normal-only. These are estimates under an artificial brightness-matched distribution, not directly observed real manufacturing FPR. A previously recorded post-hoc analysis using alternative brightness-matched calibration thresholds found recall of 96% and 91% (normal-only 63%): the recall advantage persists in that sensitivity analysis, but this does not establish how much brightness or other acquisition cues contribute. Brightness has not been shown to explain the entire recall advantage; the observed pooled FPR and the reweighted estimates describe different distributions. Box-level mAP50 was low (0.29); this study did not analyse why.
  • On a defect type absent from training, most of the advantage disappeared. For “missing”, YOLO11s caught 19/19 when the type was in training and 11/19 when it was not — about the normal-only level (10/19). For “extra”: 10/12, 9/12 and 7/12. Tiny samples, and the held-out runs also trained on slightly fewer defects. The “missing” hits without that type in training are not detections of the missing part: of 11 flagged images, 6 had a top box touching the defect and 0 had any box at IoU ≥ 0.5.
  • The normal-only number is not a verdict on normal-only methods. On PCB4 the pipeline ran without board-specific preprocessing — the protocol ruled out new PCB4 development — and with the original registration rule it did worse (50%). It shows how much the per-board adaptation done for PCB2 and PCB3 matters.
  • Engineering reading. Once representative labelled defects exist, a supervised detector is the stronger candidate for this review task on this evidence, for the defect types its labels cover. This compares two learning regimes with different label budgets, not two architectures, and it does not show that detection is better in general. Because its recall dropped to roughly the normal-only level on an unseen type, a plan for new defect types — a labelling loop, or a complementary check — is needed either way. Neither approach was tested on factory images.

Different supervision: the detectors were trained on boxes for the same board and the same defect types they were tested on; the normal-only model saw no defects. Small samples (100 defects, 255 test normals); the unseen-type rows rest on 31 images and show only gross effects. The same 255 test normals are scored by all five fold models, so pooled YOLO false alarms rest on 1,275 evaluations of 255 images, not on independent images. Latency is indicative and is not a speed ranking: median per image on one GPU, one image at a time, from file to score, but at different input sizes (YOLO 1024 px letterboxed; normal-only 768×640), with registration only in the registered variant, measured once on 50 images and, for YOLO, with one fold model. The post-hoc and audit checks were added after the results were seen; files: exploratory/yolo_pcb4/audit/. PCB4 numbers are not comparable with PCB1–PCB3 and are not an improvement over v2. Ultralytics is AGPL-3.0; it was used locally in a separate environment and is not part of the project's dependencies.

Protocol, split audit, per-image scores and analysis: exploratory/yolo_pcb4/.

4Architecture and implementation

One image in, one recommendation out. Each stage is a small module with its own unit tests; the same code serves every board type, driven by a versioned configuration file.

  1. 1RegisterFind the board by colour, correct shift and tilt, decide a half-turn by template correlation.align.py
  2. 2Crop and resizeCentred crop of the registered frame, resized to the model input.features.py
  3. 3Extract featuresFrozen ImageNet Wide-ResNet-50-2, layer2 + layer3, a fixed random subset of channels, local averaging.features.py
  4. 4Model normal appearancePer-position Gaussian of normal features; a patch's anomaly is its Mahalanobis distance.gaussian.py
  5. 5Score the imageMaximum of the smoothed anomaly map: v1 over the whole frame, v2 over the board region.roi.py
  6. 6DecideCompare with the threshold frozen on calibration normals: REVIEW or NO REVIEW.calibration.py

Image ROI — region of interest

The part of the image where the score is taken. v2 uses the maximum anomaly over a board region built from defect-free training images plus a 16-pixel margin. If less than 0.95 of an image's own board mask lies inside the region, the system does not trust it and scores the whole frame instead, which can only make a review more likely.

Evaluation harness

A single command-line tool runs every step in order — prepare, split, fit, calibrate (writes the freeze), evaluate, robustness, compare, check. evaluate refuses to run if the model, configuration or split differs from the committed freeze; check fails if any reported number does not trace to a recorded output.

5Controlled experiments and results

Each controlled change was pre-registered: hypothesis, split, endpoints and decision rule committed before the test data was opened, thresholds frozen on separate normal images, one evaluation. v2 changed one thing — scoring over the board region — and was confirmed on PCB2, a board type not used in its development.

  1. PCB2 Measured

    Board-region scoring cut false alarms

    On a held-back board type, test false alarms fell from 13% to 3% (−10 pts, CI −17 to −3); AUROC rose from 0.927 to 0.979.

    So: The change works for the problem it targeted.

  2. PCB2 Measured

    Recall did not improve

    80% of defects flagged by both versions, against a proposed 90%; the pre-registered recall hypothesis was not supported. Smallest third of defects: 56% (19/34).

    So: Detection sensitivity, not false alarms, is now the binding constraint.

  3. PCB2 Measured

    Darkening breaks the operating point

    A 10% darker, lower-contrast copy of each image raised v2 false alarms from 3.6% to 28.7%; brightening did not.

    So: Lighting must be controlled or corrected — and that must be validated — before a line trial. This motivated the PCB3 experiment.

PCB3: a pre-registered illumination-correction experiment

PCB2 showed that a 10% darker image raised false alarms by +25.1 pts. This experiment tested one candidate fix on a board type never used before, under a protocol committed before the data was opened, evaluated once. In one line: the fix did what it was designed to do, the problem it targets barely appeared on PCB3, and it introduced a new weakness.

Design (fixed before PCB3 was opened)

  • One change: standardise each image's global brightness and contrast to the training-image median, with one gain for all colour channels, before registration.
  • Baseline = v2 pipeline; candidate = v2 + correction. Same images, own thresholds, each frozen on 150 separate normal images.
  • Primary endpoint: difference-in-differences of the false-alarm rise under global darkening (G1) on 101 test + 155 holdout normals; paired bootstrap.
  • Gates: clean recall and clean false alarms must not get worse beyond fixed margins. Non-uniform lighting (N1) is the out-of-class test.
  • Known in advance: G1 is a global change, so the correction can undo it almost by construction. A good G1 result is not evidence of robustness to real lighting.

Two decisions, kept separate

A · Pre-registered experimental outcome

ROBUSTNESS IMPROVEMENT SUPPORTED — exactly as computed by the frozen rule, and weakly informative on PCB3. It says only that under a synthetic global darkening the candidate's false-alarm rise was smaller than the baseline's (−0.4 vs +4.3 pts; difference −4.7, CI −8.6 to −0.8). The baseline's own rise was below the protocol's pre-set line for an informative test.

B · Engineering adoption decision

Do not adopt the lighting correction as the preferred pipeline. It cut the brightening false-alarm rise (+15.2 → +2.7 pts) but raised false alarms under a mild blur by +14.5 pts (9/256 → 46/256 normals; baseline +0.4), beyond the original 10-point limit.

Rejecting the candidate does not approve the baseline. The baseline also fails the robustness criterion (brightening +15.2 pts), and neither variant has real end-user validation, a factory pilot or a measured operational return.

How to read it

ADid the correction fix global darkening?
Yes, for what it could fix: the candidate's rise under darkening was −0.4 pts against the baseline's +4.3 (difference −4.7 pts, CI −8.6 to −0.8). But the baseline's rise was below the pre-set line for a meaningful test, and a global darkening is exactly what a global correction undoes. This is not evidence of robustness to real lighting.
BDid registration and segmentation become more stable?
Very likely part of the effect. On training images, darkening moved the baseline's estimated board pose by 10.7 px (median) and the candidate's by 0.2 px; board-region fail-safe events 8 versus 0. The experiment cannot separate registration from feature effects, so no split is claimed.
CDid anomaly-score behaviour improve?
Clean behaviour unchanged (AUROC 0.982 → 0.983; recall 90% → 91%). Brightening: rise +15.2 → +2.7 pts. But under a mild blur the candidate's false alarms rose by +14.5 pts (9/256 → 46/256) against +0.4 for the baseline — an unplanned observation; a plausible cause is that blur lowers global contrast, which the correction then stretches.
DWhat remains under non-uniform lighting?
No improvement: difference +0.4 pts (CI −2.7 to +3.9). Both rises were small on PCB3, so the limitation rule was not triggered, but a global correction does not address a lighting gradient — as stated before the test.
EIs it ready for production-affecting deployment?
No. Against the unchanged criteria both variants are INCONCLUSIVE: clean targets are met on PCB3, but the robustness criterion fails for both (baseline under brightening, candidate under blur). The correction also adds latency (187 → 292 ms median). All perturbations were synthetic. The candidate is not adopted, and the baseline is not production-ready.

Disclosed deviation: the protocol required the PCB3 board-mask adaptation (Addendum B1) to be committed before fitting; it was decided before fitting but committed about five minutes after both models were fitted. No calibration or test image had been scored. The diagnostics and this disclosure (Addendum B2) were committed before calibration.

Technical disclosure: analysis-code repair after PCB3 testing

After the PCB3 test and holdout images had been scored once, the pre-registered paired-analysis program refused to run, and one check in it was corrected. The analysis program that produced the PCB3 result is therefore not identical to the frozen one. Nothing here is backdated.

TimeEvent
16:58Freeze committed (eb4e7a9): thresholds, configurations, split and source code
16:58–17:07Single planned evaluation of both variants. No PCB3 test or holdout image was scored after this.
17:09, 17:10Paired analysis refused twice, unchanged code: an input check required the label “anomaly”, but VisA records the defect type (bent, melt, scratch, missing).
17:14Check corrected (7dbd302). Summary test metrics had already been seen on the evaluation console.
17:15Paired analysis completed and committed (9c9f7c5).
What changed
One condition in the function that reads ground-truth masks for the descriptive small/low-contrast defect table. That table could not be produced before the repair; its arithmetic did not change.
What did not change
Model fitting, preprocessing, thresholds, test scores, predictions, the primary statistic and the decision rule. No image was re-scored and the test was not repeated.
Programmatic cross-check
A separate script that imports none of the project code recomputed every PCB3 number from the raw score files and the original masks: 90 of 90 checks agree with the recorded outputs.

Full incident record — chronology, exact patch, file hashes, deviations — in the repository at docs/pcb3_post_evaluation_repair.md; every post-test event in docs/illumination_experiment_deviations.md; the recomputation in reports/pcb3_verification/recompute.md. Times are 2026-10-09, Taiwan time.

6Failure investigation and lessons

What broke, how it was found, and what it changes. Two of the most useful findings were failures that raised no error.

  1. PCB3 Demonstrated

    Board-finding assumed a grey background

    On PCB3's saturated green cloth the original colour rule marked 96% of every frame as board, so registration silently did nothing. A hue band measured on training images restored a board mask of 15%.

    So: Background-dependent preprocessing must be re-validated at every site; it failed silently here.

  2. PCB3 Demonstrated

    Registration and the board region are only approximately portable

    Without correction, a 10% darkening moved the estimated board pose by 10.7 px (median) on training images. The board region covers 48% of the frame; about 31% of its pixels are cloth.

    So: Lint close to the board can still trigger a false alarm (see the error examples); pose estimation depends on brightness.

  3. PCB3 Measured

    A fix traded one sensitivity for another

    The lighting correction removed most of the brightening sensitivity but made a mild blur raise false alarms by +14.5 pts (baseline +0.4).

    So: Every fix is checked against the full perturbation set, not only the one it targets.

Lessons carried forward

  • Silent failures are the expensive kind: preprocessing needs output checks (mask area, coverage, fallback rate), not just successful execution.
  • Change one thing at a time and fix the analysis before the data is opened; when the plan breaks, disclose the change rather than rewrite history.
  • Keep the experimental verdict and the engineering decision separate: a rule can say “supported” while the change is still not adopted.
  • A recall measured on a hundred benchmark defects is uncertain by several points; report intervals and recall by defect size.

7Engineering discipline: built to be taken over

How this project stays understandable, reproducible and safe to change if another engineer takes it over. Every practice is marked by what is actually true: demonstrated in this repository, proposed as a team practice, or not yet implemented. Paths refer to files in the project repository.

DemonstratedProposedNot yet implemented

A

Clear ownership and traceability

Anyone can find why something was decided and who owns it.

  • Demonstrated Requirements and acceptance targets are versioned files; the targets were never edited after a result was seen. Evidence: docs/requirements.mdconfig/acceptance_criteria.yaml
  • Demonstrated Technical decisions recorded with their rationale and the alternatives rejected. Evidence: docs/engineering_decisions.mddocs/v2_decision_record.md
  • Demonstrated Every experiment has a protocol committed before its test data was opened; milestones trace to commits. Evidence: docs/v2_experiment_protocol.mddocs/illumination_experiment_protocol.mdreports/project_milestones.json
  • Proposed Named owners for the configuration, the acceptance targets and the operating threshold. The roles are defined; no person is assigned yet. Evidence: docs/handoff.md
B

Controlled changes

Nothing that affects a result changes silently.

  • Demonstrated One controlled change per version or experiment, compared against the unchanged pipeline on the same images. Evidence: docs/v2_decision_record.mddocs/illumination_experiment_protocol.md
  • Demonstrated Configurations and thresholds versioned and hashed at freeze; evaluation refuses a changed model, configuration or split, or an uncommitted freeze. Evidence: config/pcb2_v2.yamlreports/pcb2_v2/frozen_operating_point.jsonsrc/ivad/pipeline.py
  • Demonstrated Deviations from a protocol recorded with timestamps and disclosed, never backdated. Evidence: docs/illumination_experiment_deviations.mddocs/pcb3_post_evaluation_repair.md
  • Proposed Human peer review of every change, with a blocking finding tied to the exact commit it was raised on and cleared only by a review of the new commit.
  • Not yet implemented Human peer review has not taken place: review so far is programmatic and AI-assisted, and the owner's review is pending.
C

Automated quality gates

Claims are checked by code, not by reading.

  • Demonstrated Unit, integration and synthetic end-to-end tests, including the website and PDF builds. Evidence: tests/
  • Demonstrated Data-leakage safeguards: split audited with file hashes; thresholds set only on calibration normals; test images scored once. Evidence: manifests/split_pcb2_audit.jsonsrc/ivad/data.py
  • Demonstrated Numerical consistency: every reported number traces to a recorded output; a separate script recomputes PCB3 without the project code. Evidence: src/ivad/consistency.pyverification/recompute_pcb3.py
  • Demonstrated Reproducible environment: locked dependencies; a clean-environment rerun of PCB1 v1 was byte-identical. Evidence: requirements.lock.txtdocs/handoff.md
  • Not yet implemented Continuous integration: the gates are run locally; no server runs them on every change yet.
D

Maintainability and handoff

The next engineer can run it, debug it and roll it back.

  • Demonstrated Handoff guide: how to run and reproduce, configuration ownership, known failure modes, support considerations. Evidence: docs/handoff.md
  • Demonstrated Fail-safe behaviour in code: a board that cannot be found raises an error; an untrusted board region falls back to the more conservative full-frame score. Evidence: src/ivad/align.pysrc/ivad/roi.py
  • Proposed Monitoring of review rate, fallback rate and brightness drift; rollback to the previous model and threshold, which every freeze keeps. Evidence: docs/handoff.md
  • Not yet implemented A runbook for a live line, factory monitoring and incident handling: none of this has been operated anywhere.

The first commit already contains a working prototype; earlier local work is not separately timestamped, and no total delivery time is claimed. Exact commit times and hashes are kept in the repository's audit history.

8Technical readiness and AI Engineering handoff

Technical feasibility is demonstrated on public data. Further real-world validation is proposed. Production-affecting use is not yet justified.

Demonstrated Technical feasibility on public benchmark images

  • Normal-only detector, registration and board-region scoring, implemented and unit-tested.
  • PCB2 confirmatory run: false alarms 13% → 3%, recall 80% in both versions.
  • Robustness to synthetic lighting, blur and shift measured at frozen thresholds.
  • PCB3 pre-registered illumination-correction experiment, run once; the correction is not adopted.

Proposed Real-world validation

  • Site requirements confirmed by the quality owner: must-catch defect types and sizes, review capacity, cost of a miss versus a review.
  • Shadow mode on real line images, affecting no decision.
  • The site checks below as entry gates before any decision is influenced by the tool.
  • A second Go/No-Go on that evidence.

Not yet validated Beyond what this project can show

  • Any factory image, camera, lamp, line speed or real defect mix.
  • Usability of the review interface; reviewer agreement.
  • Labour saving or financial return.
  • Robustness to real (not synthetic) lighting changes.

Remaining technical risks

  • Detection: PCB2 recall 80% against a proposed 90%; smallest third of defects 56%.
  • Lighting: a 10% darker image raised PCB2 false alarms by +25.1 pts; brighter images raised PCB3 false alarms by +15.2 pts.
  • Portability: on a green background the original board-finding rule marked 96% of the frame as board.

What a new site or line must prove

PCB1, PCB2 and PCB3 are board types from a public dataset, not manufacturing sites. They still show, concretely, which assumptions break when anything changes.

RiskWhat this project observedWhat a new site must provide or pass
Background-dependent board segmentationGrey cloth worked; PCB3's green cloth made the original rule mark 96% of the frame as board, with no error raised.Segmentation check on the site's own normal images: board-mask area within an expected range, visual sign-off of a contact sheet.
Lighting sensitivityPCB2 false alarms rose by +25.1 pts under a 10% darkening; on PCB3, brightness changes also moved the estimated board pose.Lighting specification and a brightness/contrast check on every image; a perturbation test at the site's frozen threshold.
Orientation and placement19% of PCB1 boards were turned half a round; placement varied on every board type.Fixture or registration acceptance: pose spread on site normals, no wrong-orientation decisions on a labelled sample.
ROI compatibilityThe board region covered 48% of the PCB3 frame with about 31% cloth inside; false alarms can start on cloth near the board.Region built from the site's own normals, coverage gate passing, fail-safe rate on calibration images below the agreed limit.
Small and low-contrast defectsSmallest third of PCB2 defects: 56% recall.A labelled sample of the site's real defect mix; recall per size class reported, not just overall.
Site-specific data and calibrationEvery board type needed its own fitted model, board region and threshold.Enough normal images for fit and a separate set for calibration; a held-out set the team never looks at during tuning.
Threshold and model versioningEvaluation refuses to run if the model, config or split changed after the freeze, or if the freeze is not committed.Versioned model + threshold + config released together; any change triggers recalibration and a regression run.

What an AI Engineering team would need to implement it

Documented in the repository's handoff guide; none of it has been operated on a line.

Camera and input specification
One RGB image of one board, fixed overhead camera, the same board type and background as the fitted model. Other inputs are out of scope.
Input-quality checks
Proposed: compare each image's brightness, contrast and focus with the training range and route outliers to review, because measured false alarms rise sharply under darkening.
Registration and ROI reliability
No board found raises an error, never a silent pass. If the board mask is not inside the board region, the whole-frame score is used (more conservative). Fallback rate is a monitored quantity; calibration stops if it exceeds its limit.
Model and threshold versioning
Model, threshold, config and split are hashed at freeze; evaluation refuses mismatches. Every release carries its freeze record.
Site-specific evaluation
Each new board, background, camera or lamp is fitted, calibrated and evaluated on its own data, with a held-out set nobody tunes on.
Monitoring and regression tests
Track review rate, fallback rate, brightness drift and reviewer-confirmed false alarms per shift. Unit, end-to-end and consistency tests re-run on every change.
Rollback and incident handling
Keep the previous model and threshold set deployable; roll back on a review-rate or fallback-rate alarm, then recalibrate offline. The tool only recommends; unclear cases and any suspected systematic miss go to the quality owner.
Handoff documentation
How to run and reproduce, known failure modes, configuration ownership and licensing notes are in the repository's handoff guide.

Production deployment needs real operational constraints and representative factory data, including capture conditions, must-catch defects and review capacity, before technical acceptance criteria can be validated.

Terms used on this page
Recall
Share of defective boards the tool sends to human review.
False-alarm rate
Share of normal boards the tool sends to review. The tool only recommends a review, so a false alarm costs reviewer time, not product.
AUROC
Threshold-free ranking quality: the probability that a random defective board scores higher than a random normal one.
Frozen threshold (P95)
The score above which an image is flagged, set from separate normal images to target about 5% false alarms, and fixed before any test image is scored.
Pre-registration
Writing the hypothesis, data split, endpoint and decision rule into the repository before the test data is opened.
Difference-in-differences
How much less (or more) the candidate's false alarms rise under a perturbation than the baseline's, on the same images.
Shadow mode
Running the tool alongside existing inspection without affecting any decision, to measure it on real production images.
Out-of-fold
In cross-validation, a score given to an image by the model that was not trained on it.
